item.title: Website - Cosmic Nomad – 12 July 2015
item.description:
Hey Patrons!

It’s been a big month of writing, and with all the self-reflection going on I’ve been reminded recently about the last time I was flat-out writing and self reflecting on everything going on: writing “Cosmic Nomad” while I was living and working in Melbourne during 2015.

Truth be told in 2014 I was completely done with comedy shows. I was less than happy with how “Becoming Martian” had turned out, being too dry, impersonal, and simply not funny enough. I was in the final stages of the world tour of “Becoming Martian”, travelling around Australia talking about using comedy to share space science but already committed to personally moving away from stand-up, and had been invited to speak and run a workshop at the National Young Writer’s Festival – the last official stop of the tour and one I’ve written about before.

item.title: Website - Exciting & Unpredictable – 25 November 2014
item.description:
Hey Patrons!

As you probably read from the earlier post about WOMADelaide, things have been pretty chaotic the last few weeks. I’m always amused by the strange cycles that these things seem to take – how I’ll swing from long stretches of quiet into intense periods that vary in length from weeks to months.

The tension and release is important, because while I’d love to just keep going and going and going, there needs to be time to stop and reassess what you’re doing too. It also seems partially disconnected from my own personal stability too: January and February may have been emotionally turbulent but they were also painfully quiet in terms of work. Meanwhile March has been both incredibly busy and absolutely amazing!

item.title: Website - Mischief in 2017
item.description:
So I thought I’d share a little of what is going on here at the moment, because it’s driving me a little nuts waiting to hear back on some amazing opportunities for 2017 as even MORE amazing opportunities pop up to complicate things even further!

Some of you might have seen some press in the last day or so saying I’ll be speaking at the WOMADelaide festival in March alongside the commander of NASA’s recent 12-month Hi-SEAS mission, Carmel Johnston. It’s been a few months in the planning, and I’m incredibly excited about the extraordinary opportunity to speak at the Planet Talks with some absolutely incredibly people… but I haven’t promoted it heavily yet. I’ve got an interview about it with ABC radio in a little over an hour, and I’m kind of reluctant to do it (even though I know the interviewer and know it will be great).

item.title: Website - Partner Parallels, Growth & Foreshadowing – 25 September 2015
item.description:
Hey everyone,

The last few weeks have been incredibly turbulent. Between a mountain of chaos with school visits gone wrong, being knocked back for science communication work in Australia at the same time as incredible offers for work overseas, leading me to question whether I should keep trying to make a difference in my home country… I’ve also had someone who I honestly never thought I’d see again come back into my life. And just as quickly as she reappeared, it now looks like she’ll disappear from it again.

item.title: Website - Reading, Watching & Listening – December 2016
item.description:
Hey Patreons! I’m still getting the hang of the way Patreon works, but I figured the first thing I’d share as a members-only exclusive would be a round-up of what I’m reading, watching and listening to at the moment. Let me know what you think in the comments below!

Books I’m reading
I’ve always loved reading, but it’s almost exclusively for learning as I’ve struggled reading non-fiction ever since I was a kid. Having the “Read the All-Time Greatest Books” on my 101 Things list set the challenge to change that, and when I bought a Kindle about 4 years back I made a concerted effort to learn to appreciate more literature. The challenges of working & travelling around the world this year meant my Kindle spent a lot of this year uncharge in my pack, and when I finally charged it on the way back to Australia I found the screen had been crushed! Luckily someone gave me a new kindle as an early Xmas present, so I’m back into it again each night before bed.

item.title: Website - Reading, Watching & Listening – February 2017
item.description:
Hey Patreons! I’m up in Indonesia and Malaysia at the moment – taking a break to to to sort some things out emotionally and mentally before this year really kicks into high gear. I’ll be back next week though so I’m excited to see what happens later this month, because we’re certainly in for a big one!

Books I’m reading
With all the political madness going on the US and Australia at the moment it’s been incredibly easy to be pulled into tracking the latest horror in the news on Twitter, and while it’s important to stay up to date it started to become all consuming last month. To try and counteract my endless and concerned scrolling, coupled with a clear despondency I’ve been fighting for the last few months, I decided to get myself back on track by laying out a list of what I need to do to feel ready for Mars One selection in the second half of this year.

item.description:
Hey Patrons,
I tend not to talk about religion too much, mostly because I’ve had a lot of different experiences that make having a quick and easy discussion about it very difficult. It’s also not something I think anyone SHOULD have a quick and easy discussion about.

Maybe I’ll write more about it at a later date with a solid look at how I see different religions as just a cultural filter for viewing the universe and comprehending our role in it… but for now I wanted to share a little something I just sent to God. item.title: Website - Getting to Mars Part 3
item.description:
We kicked off my series on “Getting to Mars” last time with a look at Orbital Mechanics – showing that the physics of getting from one planet to another can be mostly explained with a stapler, a pen, and Kristen Wiig looking unimpressed. This time we’re looking at the propulsion systems that we’ll use to get to Mars.

Of course because every armchair expert has their own pet propulsion project they think is critical to the future of space exploration, this is probably the article I’ll have to delete the most hate-mail for. That’s right – I don’t even read your unsolicited and poorly-spelled bullshit before deleting it, but thank you for reading all of mine! And if you haven’t already figured it out this is also the article you’re probably going to get me at my snarkiest, because there are three phrases I hear on a fairly regular basis that genuinely get under my skin and strangely all three are connected in some way to spacecraft propulsion…

item.title: Website - Getting to Mars Part 2
item.description: There’s a common misconception among the general public that physics is boring, yet nothing could be further from the truth. As a physicist I can say with confidence physics is awesome, it’s just physics teachers that are boring.I hesitate to say all physics teachers are boring, because I’ve met a few really exceptional ones… but there’s also been plenty of others who some how manage to suck all the colour and joy out of the incredible relationships that govern our universe. So with this in mind we’re going to tackle arguably one of the most abstract, mathematically complex, and potentially boring concepts in Newtonian physics – Orbital Mechanics – and we’re going to make it awesome instead.

item.title: Website - Why I don't get invited to writers festivals anymore
item.description: In October 2014 I was at the National Young Writer’s Festival in Newcastle, standing awkwardly by the snacks at the opening Meet and Greet event and trying to decide who looked friendly enough to fulfill the “Meet” component of this little soiree. By blocking the corn chips just long enough I accidentally made eye-contact with someone after a nacho cheese fix, introduced myself, then asked what she was doing at the festival: “I’m a poet. I’m running two workshops and doing a late night reading. What about you?” I told her, to which she replied “You’re not an astronaut – that is THE WORST pickup line I’ve ever heard”, then stalked off with corn chip dust all over her fingers and nose.

item.title: Website - Getting to Mars Part 1
item.description: For the last few years I’ve structured my school visits and public talks primarily around answering questions about the Mars One project, rather than lecturing. For an average 90 minute school visit for example I’ll usually only speak for the first 10-15 minutes – with plenty of images of Mars and no text on the slides – before spending the next 75-80 minutes answering every question under the Sun about life on Mars. School visits in particular are incredibly entertaining, mostly because kids have absolutely no shame and no chill – they will ask absolutely every obscene thing you could ever imagine, while literally bouncing up and down in their chair with excitement, and I have to try to honestly answer their question about how sex, death, shitting, and/or cannibalism will be different on Mars than it is on Earth while their teachers look on in horror.

item.title: Website - Dear Josh in 2020
item.description:
Dear Josh in 2020,
Firstly congratulations if you’re still around to read this – given all the stupid shit you’ve done through the years it’s a genuine surprise you’re still here to write this in 2016 at all, let alone read it in 2020. That’s not to say you’ve stopped doing stupid shit, because in case you’ve forgotten, you still do. A lot. But atleast over the last 4 years since you first found out about Mars One you’ve been a hell of a lot more focused on why you take ridiculous risks than you ever were. There’s a reason to take risks now… even if that reason is so I can live on a cold and unforgiving planet 56 million kilometers away without hope of return. I also spend a lot less time screaming at audiences while wearing a koala suit & playing ukulele now too, which I’m sure most people will agree is a good thing.

item.title: Website - Good Bad Ugly (Mars One Update)
item.description:
There’s been a mountain of recent updates on Mars One over the last few months, so I figured it’d be a a great opportunity to kick off the regular “Space” posts with a full-spectrum round-up of the good, bad and ugly of all that’s happened.

The Good

After a huge amount of initial support and media coverage Mars One has had a really hard time transitioning from a small space startup with an incredible idea into a functioning space company with revenue stable enough to take that incredible idea further. After limping along with a small team trying to make ends meet while encouraging top-end investors to finance a significant proportion of the whole project, the merchandise store and private investment have generated a steady baseline stream of income over the last 3 years and provided the financial evidence of the business plan smaller investors needed.

item.title: Website – Diving between continents & hiking to desolation Iceland
item.description: While there’s been a rough plan on where to go and what to do this trip since July last year, I’ve deliberately held off booking things too far in advance to keep myself open to random opportunities along the way. So a week before I was slated to fly from Dublin to Boston I decided I should actually book the flight, and was in for one hell of a surprise. Far and away the cheapest option was to go via Reykjevic, and after the Ethiopia episode there was NO way I was going to fly all the way to Iceland to spend the entire time in the airport again. Even if it DID have free wifi. So I booked flights and set 4 days aside to explore the land of fire & ice. I woke up in Dublin the day before the flight to Reykjavic cheerful, bouncing out of bed ready for the next adventure and put the kettle on for my morning coffee. Waiting for it to boil, my stomach suddenly dropped as I realised: – I don’t speak Icelandic, – I’m travelling so light I don’t even have a jumper, and – I actually have no idea what the hell to do in Iceland for 4 days. My entire knowledge of Iceland in 4 minutes & 7 seconds After some furious research I created something vaguely resembling a plan, made a couple of bookings, was given a jumper, and figured if it all went horribly wrong at least my frozen corpse would be cryogenically preserved striking an awesome pose inside some Icelandic glacier. Hopefully long enough there’s been 3 or 4 alien invasions to really clear the place out before I’m revived First impression flying into Iceland was that it’s not… really… inviting… Unless you’re really into lifeless volcanic outcroppings Also turns out you don’t fly into Reykjavik: you fly into Keflavik, out on the Reykjanik peninsula about 50km away from Reykjavik. Which suited me just fine, as where I’d hired a campervan from was right near the airport and I’d had more than enough of seeing/hearing/smelling/tasting people over the last few months – avoiding the capital fitted well with my plan to escape humans for at least a few days. Picking up my “Happy Camper”, I decided to test out this whole “driving on the right-hand side of the road business” by driving around the local neighborhood to get the hang of having everything reversed. After driving the back streets (only going around a roundabout the wrong way once) I managed to grab camping food for the next 3 days from the local supermarket (using a combination of mime & animal noises to communicate with the cashier who spoke perfect English) and found an awesome Viking statue. My bird, beard & axe game are severely lacking here Emboldened by my Viking brethren, it was time to start the adventure and venture out onto the highway: I was on it 2 minutes before I stalled the camper trying to take an exit, stranding me halfway across a dual-carriageway on a blind corner. The camper refused to start, the car behind me started beeping, I threw on the hazard lights sending the car behind me into a blind honking-rage, before the engine eventually restarted on the 6th go and I pulled clear of an oncoming semi-trailer. Glad to say the driving for the rest of the trip was relatively uneventful… Rather than racing to all the usual tourist spots I wanted to get out and away from people (especially ones driving other vehicles). Hafnir was relatively close, on the coast, and sounded vaguely like the name of a battlemech in Mechwarrior (because I’m psychologically 7 years old). And as you’d expect from a place I randomly chose based on its tenuous link to a video game I played 15 years ago, there was nothing to see except the set of Biodome 2. Pauly Shore films don’t get the budgets they used to But just down the coast was a place where you could walk across a bridge connecting the North American & Eurasian continental plates… Shout out to my high school geography teacher who said “plate tectonics are just a theory”… just like gravity And another place called Gunnuhver, where the Icelandic believe a demonic ghost lives and geothermal steam jets out of the ground (these two things are probably connected). “Please don’t shove your face in the vent of stones producing super-heated steam that we named after a demon” Working my way around the peninsula, I found myself being followed by a pair of German tourists. This became a common theme during my time in Iceland whenever I was on any of the “ring” roads – the same people stopping to look at the same incredibly stunning scenery you stopped to look at, leaving after about the same amount of time it took you to get bored with it, before driving in the same direction and turning up to ruin your next stop with their peopleness. The Atlantic Ocean – largely untainted by peopleness We reached peak peopleness when I stopped at the Blue Lagoon. The Blue Lagoon itself held little to no appeal to me, but everyone raves about it being a “must visit” and it was on my way, so I figured I’d at least call in to see what all the fuss was about. And lo and behold, it’s a pale blue lagoon. Please hold your gasps of shock & astonishment It was also terrifyingly touristy. The whole place was setup like a hotel-resort, funneling everyone into a lobby and restaurant, charged access to swim in the lake, and you literally had to exit via gift shop. And every asshole in Iceland was there with their obnoxious screaming kids. I snapped a selfie as evidence I’d been there (above), used their marble toilets and bolted out of there. How’s the serenity? The whole point of spending a few days in a camper driving around Iceland was that I didn’t have to interact with people if I didn’t want to (I didn’t), and I could disconnect from the rest of the world to enjoy the natural beauty of Iceland. So I connected my SIM-less phone to the stereo, put the Martian soundtrack on loop, and followed the south coast. The camper hire guy had said I’d get around Iceland a lot quicker than I might expect, and he was dead right – I’d driven half the south coast before midday, and my only plan had been to drive that before heading to Thingvellir national park to camp overnight ready for my dive at Silfra the next morning. So with about 11 hours of sunlight left (welcome to the land of the midnight sun) I headed inland towards Geysir instead, where the word “geyser” comes from. The Icelandic are a very literal people With the icy wind blowing off the mountains, I decided to have my first meal in the camper – cracking the side door just enough not to gas myself on the stove fumes but without freezing either. It’s a delicate balance being this classy After another venture into a hyper-touristy hotel/resort at Geysir – to abuse a toilet, drain the dregs of my 2-minute noodle soup out in the car park, then leave again – I decided “national park” sounded like the place likely to have the lowest peopleness. Heading south-west into Thingvellir national park, you can see why they filmed Game of Thrones here. I think. I mean, I’ve never watched it and never plan to, but I know there’s a bunch of medieval families straight up murdering each other at an awesome wedding, and vague claims of dragons. Which all sounds like it should be filmed in the same place Vikings came from. It also probably explains why the show “Vikings” is filmed here. Which I’ve also never seen. Probably because I’m too busy visiting these places instead of watching shows filmed here There was still plenty of light when I parked at Silfra – where I’d be diving the next morning – so I decided to have a look around. Walking along a path through a schism in the sheer rock face, I turned around and saw this… All of the pretty … about 10 seconds before another tourist walked up to me and said “Excuse me, do you know which side is North America?”. Just like the bridge between two continents, Thingvellir national park is situated right where the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates are pulling apart. I worked out we were facing North and told him “The mountains on the left”. All that smart ass geography knowledge didn’t mean a damn when it came to settle in for the night though – the guy who hired me the camper told me that “most campsites are open all year round” but do you think I could find one with an unlocked toilet and shower? After driving around the whole park I eventually found one that at least had the disable toilet unlocked, and seems like it was the only one in the region too because I had multiple people knock on my camper door around twilight asking if I’d seen any other sites with unlocked toilets and showers. So much for escaping peopleness. I’d be in for a little more peopleness the next morning, but it’d all be worth it though: I’d be taking the plunge at one of the top 10 dive sites in the world. While all of Thingvillir national park is formed by the North American & Eurasian tectonic plates pulling apart, Silfra is the spot in Thingvillir where water running off the mountains emerges after 75+ years of limestone filtering to form a freshwater lake. So besides the fact you’re diving between two continents, you’re also diving in the highest visibility water in the world (measured at over 120m/393ft), and it feels a bit like you’re spacewalking instead of diving. Camping just up the road meant I was there before all the divers driving from Reykjevik, so I chatted to our surface support instructor Tanya while she set the gear up & we waited. I was qualified as a TDI Advanced Trimix diver and instructing for both PADI & SSI prior to moving to the UK to join the Royal Marines, but I really haven’t been diving regularly since then. So while the knowledge & experience are all still there I was definitely rusty, and it was great having the team from DIVE.IS looking after us. The water at Silfra is also about 2°C, which meant wearing some incredibly sexy dry suits… Dry suit is borrowed but the sexy beanie is all mine. I was grouped up with Johnathon (an English uni student who’d just done his Open Water course in the Red Sea) and Pien (an Californian lady who was only on her 4th dive ever) to be led by our dive guide Rob who’d just finished a season instructing and leading dives through the WW1 German wrecks at Scarpa Flow (one of my all-time “places to dive before I die/go to Mars”). Our first dive was really just a check out so we could get used to the dry suits, but it was still extraordinary. Pien struggled with her buoyancy & ears, so Rob spent most of the dive looking after her. I kept a casual eye on Johnno at the same time, but he adapted to the dry suit really quickly so we spent most of the dive soaking up as much of the underwater scenery as we could. It was still bloody cold though, and after the first dive and a hot chocolate on the surface Pien was so cold she decided to skip the 2nd dive. Which is a shame because it’s when Rob, Johnno & I got the best pictures, like hanging onto two continents at once… North American plate in my left hand, Eurasia in my right … and diving on something that felt like a blue-tinged moonscape. You can check out the full gallery here, but it’s safe to say the experience was absolutely extraordinary. After swapping cards and hugging a huge thanks to everyone, it was off on the next adventure into the Icelandic highlands! In July 2015 Mars One’s CEO Bas Lansdorp was scouting locations for a mock Mars habitat, and posted photos & coordinates for two possible sites in Iceland – one near Vik, and the other in the highlands near Suðurland. So I figured if I was in the country and it was so easy to get around I’d check them out myself, starting with the Suðurland site. Welcome to the Icelandic Highlands Turns out driving around Iceland is really easy  unless you want to drive on an “F-Road”. I can think of a few things the F stands for, but basically you’re not able – physically or legally – to drive on an F-Road unless you’re in something that is half 4WD & half monster truck. Do your wheels even lift bro? There’s no way my puny campervan was going to cut it, but sure enough as I pulled up at the sign marking the start of the F-road the camper’s Tom Tom was telling me the Mars One site was another 8km ahead. What the Tom Tom wasn’t telling me though was that I’d be slogging the whole way through about 2 feet of snow drift to get there. There’s no doubt it was cold when I started the hike, but it was less than 20 minutes before I was stripping out of my thermals down to a shirt & jeans. And hour & a half later I was walking around in circles trying to get a GPS lock on the coordinates Bas had shared… … before finally finding the right spot It’s difficult to describe just how desolate the whole area is. Besides some power lines way off to East that you really have to look for to see, there’s no sign of humanity or life generally. I’d kept my headphones in during the hike there, and was dumbfounded by how still & quiet the place was when turned the music off. As in eerily quiet – no wind, no birds, nothing. After snapping my photo in a place specifically selected for its barren emptiness, it was time to hike back to the camper. With everything covered in snow and no frame of reference I’d had a nightmare trying to navigate in, but using the power lines and the hill I’d climbed to get to the plateau as a heading the return journey was much quicker… and also lead me straight towards a cliff I’d skirted on the way in. After some improvised tobogganing (eg. holding my bag to my chest and sliding on my ass down 200m of snow drift) I managed to get back to the river just a kilometer from where I’d parked. The snow on the right is a LOT higher than it looks So after about 4 hours of hiking and without another soul for at least 10km, I figured a trip to Iceland wouldn’t be complete without a skinny dip in water that was flowing off highland glaciers. I could say this has been tastefully cropped, but the 2 degree water made overexposure less of an issue There was fair bit of light when I got back to the camper, so I figured I’d at least try to get to the other Mars One site at Vik too. Heading back down from the highlands and toward the southern coast both fuel and light were getting very low, but I still stopped to grab a photo of this little gem. The hotel of my people By the time I nursed the car into the service station at Vik and figured out the bizarre payment system for fuel it was well and truly twilight, and there was no way I’d be able to find the second Mars One site in the dark. I’d driven passed some amazing waterfalls and watched the sunset on Eyjafjallajökull (the volcano that shut down air traffic in Europe for 6 days in 2010) and Katla (Eyjafjallajökull’s much bigger sister), so I headed back towards the camping grounds I’d seen on the way to Vik – trying to find somewhere with very few lights in the vain hope of spotting the aurora. With total cloud cover the aurora was a no-show, but unbeknownst to me I wound up parking for the night with a waterfall directly behind me… … and one of Iceland’s most famous waterfalls a short walk away. Seljalandsfoss waterfall looking glorious And as you’d expect from one of Iceland’s most famous waterfalls, the place was packed with tourists. After a few photos of the waterfall (and dunking my head in a stream as a pseudo-shower) I scampered out of there pretty quick. But with the drive/hike in the highlands and a few nights to myself without wifi, I’d had something of a breather from peopleness. After a gorgeous drive to Selfoss through the southern mountains and skimming the edge of Reykjavik, it was time to drive back to Keflavik and return the camper. I stayed the night in a place about 9km from the airport, watching The Expanse till midnight & waiting for it to get dark enough to finally catch the aurora. But even with clear skies it never really got dark enough before the sun was coming back up again, so I guess I’ll just have to come back when the nights are longer! And probably stay in one of these bubbles for it The next day it was time to say goodbye to Iceland, so after a slow start & an awesome breakfast I figured I had plenty of time to skip the taxi and walk to the airport – popping the headphones back in and starting the hour & a half walk. I’d been warned by a friend who’s a huge Kim Kardashian fan (don’t worry, I judge her too) that Kim & Kanye were in Iceland at the same time, and low and behold just as I was walking passed the end of the runway I had their private jet take off right over my head. Personally I’m just really glad Yeezy didn’t decide to flush at the same time. Please don’t There’s been so much happening I’m about 3 weeks behind on these posts (currently in Washington D.C ahead of the Humans 2 Mars conference starting Tuesday). But the next step was flying into Boston for a few days before a weird weekend in NYC, and without going into details a lot has changed personally since I got through that. Spending 6 days being a complete space geek in Florida certainly helped too – the trip feels very much like it’s “mine” now. So I’m looking forward to getting those trip entries written & published in the next few days too 😀 - Dave Looking good mate - Josh Thanks Dad 🙂 - Mandi Ryan I’m really enjoying your posts Josh. Great to see what you are up to. Hope everything else goes well too! - Josh Cheers Mardi – there’s plenty more to follow! - Shelley Richards Is it weird if your Mum posts comments too? It is, isn’t it? Oh well, here goes: loved reading this one Josh and missing having regular contact with you but great to know that you are (again/still) exploring the big wide world. x - Josh Haha, more than OK Mum 😀 Great speaking to you both this today, and I’ll try to call a little more regularly than I have. ### Recent Posts - News – The best, the worst, & the breather [Florida] - News – Space museum overload & Mars One meetups [Washington D.C.] - News – Boston Buddies, Space Shuttles & Bottoming Out [Boston & NYC] - News – Diving between continents & hiking to desolation [Iceland] - News – Airport Hell, Involuntary Weight Loss, & UK Mars100 Meetup - News – Life in a Box, Festival Madness & Going Global - News – 2016 “Cosmic Nomad” Global Tour - News – The Martian Stunt #bringhimhome - SHSSP16 Week 3 – Fighting Flat Earthers, New Management & Cultured Chaos - SHSSP Week 2 – Goodbye Spaceman, Buzz Day & Payload Tension - SHSSP Week 1 – Droids, Starmen & Grabthar’s Hammer - News – That whole “Moving to the other side of the country” thing - News – Helena National Science Week Tour - Mars One – Parachuting & Media Mayhem - Mars Project – You Are Go To Continue Descent… - News – 2015: The Year Space Kicks It Up a Notch - Random – Fringe World for People Who Aren’t Old & Boring - Random – An Open Letter to Myself in 2020 - News – There and back again… (Part 2: Australia) - News – There and back again… Part 1: Europe

item.title: Website – That whole “Moving to the other side of the country” thing
item.description: I have no idea where to even begin describing the roller-coaster my last 5 months have been, so let’s start with the basics. I Moved to Melbourne Yup, up and left. No real warning – just gone. Leaving Perth had been in the works since the start of 2015, and given I’d been visiting Melbourne at least once a month since November it made sense it’d be where I wound up… but I sure as hell wasn’t expecting it to happen so fast. The plan had been to visit Tasmania for a holiday in late April, return to Perth to close out a few things and say goodbye, then leave on May 31st – the day before the Sunday Times named me in their list “75 People who make WA great”. Instead what happened was: - Mid April I off-handedly applied for a job in Melbourne as a school lab technician, - The school interviewed me via Skype 5 days later, - They gave me the job an hour after the interview, - I flew to Tasmania for 3 days, - Then flew from Hobart to Melbourne and started work at the school the next day The whole thing – from applying to starting work – took less than 2 weeks. With that rush I wasn’t fully prepared for when I got here, so for the first month I was commuting 2 hours a day to get to a job I’d initially thought was a part-time, but was actually full-time – 8 hours a day, 5 days a week. Needless to say it was one hell of an adjustment. As with everything though, once you’re over the initial shock and start to figure things out, you adapt and problem-solve. Learning Melbourne’s public transport system, buying a bike, and moving into an amazing share-house in Carlton solved the commuting issues – 10 minute bike ride to one school campus, and a 10 minutes walk to the other. Convenience, bitches I switched to part-time work My lab tech job was a lifesaver initially – it got me out of Perth, used my degree and chemistry knowledge, and paid far more than I’d been paid by any job since I left the mining industry. But the plan had always been to work part-time – just enough to pay the bills so I could focus my time and energy on writing & speaking about space. That is what I’d wanted to move to Melbourne for. So while my job was pretty easy – I had far too much free time – and ticked a lot of boxes, being full-time wasn’t really letting me do what I’d moved here to do. It also added evidence to the idea I’m a cartoon character… After a visit to the Victorian Space Science Education Centre (VSSEC) and bumping into a friend in science communication, I decided I’d prefer the uncertainty of casual science communication work than keep going in a secure job that stopped me from doing all the cool stuff I really wanted to do. Rather than leaving immediately and leaving the school in a lurch, I told the school I’d stay the 6 weeks till the end of Term 3 – that way they had plenty of time to find a replacement for the start of Term 4 & I had a regular pay-check while I found something more suitable. The school started planning for my departure, and I started looking for a casual science job in between working and organising everything for National Science Week … until a week later when the principal struck on the genius idea of having me go part-time. It’s a great job, but it doesn’t need someone full-time – the reality is I was bored and frustrated that I had to be there 5 days a week. So now I’m on 3.5 days a week I’ve got the part-time job I was after, I’ve reclaimed the time & energy I needed to write (hence why you’re reading this), and the school has an enthusiastic lab technician who’s excited to be there rather than wishing he was doing something else. It also means I can keep riding to work four mornings a week: one hand on the handlebars, the other casually holding a soy latte like a job-less hipster. But of course right when all this job mischief was being discussed, I was also preparing for National Science Week… Helena Payload’s National Science Week Tour In case you missed it here, here, here, or any one of the dozen other places it was covered by the global media, I helped UWA’s Motorsport Team develop a payload for Mars One’s University Competition this time last year. What you might not know (because I never mentioned it until the previous post) is that the fine folks at Inspiring Australia gave us $15,000 to travel around the country during National Science Week to speak about Helena’s development and the experience of working on an aerospace engineering project. So Andre Van Vulpen, Rowan Heinrich, Claire Quy, and I bundled off for a flash tour of the country – taking in Perth, Hobart, Adelaide, Sydney and Melbourne. Speaking about Mars One at Hobart’s Festival of Bright Ideas Slipping away from the festival to visit Mt Wellington The Helena Team together at the University of South Australia In Adelaide, setting up our first presentation In Sydney to speak at OrbitOz Speaking at Uni High in Melbourne Speaking at Simonds Catholic College in Melbourne The Helena Team after our last presentation Speaking about Mars One at Monash University The chaos didn’t stop for me there though – while the rest of the team was flying back to Perth, I was running my “How To Become An Astronaut” workshop at Laneway Learning’s Science Spectacular, and the next evening I was presenting on the International Space University’s Southern Hemisphere Summer Space Program at RMIT’s Aerospace Industry Night. And somewhere in there I turned 30 too. Becoming Adult(ish) and doing Adult(ish) things Apparently 30 is some sort of arbitrary figure where ordinary people grow up emotionally, settle into a safe and secure job, get married, have 2.4 kids, and start the slow descent into death by mediocrity. But because I’m awesome and intend to die on a different planet to the one I was born on, I turned 30 and got a tattoo of a 7-leaf clover; 100 points if you get why this is about Mars … and because I’m wildly irresponsible I had a robot spaceman tattooed on my right ass cheek at the same time; By this point you might suspect I watch a lot of Futurama. You would be correct. Turning my life back into one long punch-line In July Mars One announced that the final astronaut selection phase will take place in September 2016. The candidates knew there were two possible selection periods (March or September 2016), and after being on this roller-coaster for nearly 3 years already a big part of me was hoping they’d go with March. But instead of being frustrated by another 6 months, I’ve realised  I’ve got another 6 months to do all the stupid shit I want to do from the 101 Things list and write/tour a new comedy show about it. So now the race is on: since July I’ve attended a film premiere (#44), gotten a tattoo (#75), and I’m still chipping away at the greatest books list (#52). This whole website is due for some serious renovation, and updating the 101 Things list is the first thing to be updated. It’ll continue to be updated too as I do more stupid shit from the list when I return to full-time comedy next year. I’m currently writing my next science-comedy show “Cosmic Nomad”, so I’ll leaving my lab tech job (properly this time) at the end of 2015 to perform the show throughout 2016 – touring all the way around this shiny blue-green ball we call Earth until the final selection phase in September. The details of the tour are are still being worked out, but I’ll share them here as soon as everything is confirmed. In the meantime keep an eye out as I start to publish chapters from “Becoming Martian”; the book I wrote last year on how humans will change in physically, psychologically and culturally by colonising Mars. After sitting on the manuscript for 12 months I’ve decided I’d rather it be available for free online, rather than have it remain unread on my hard drive waiting for a publisher to wave a magic wand over it. And who knows – maybe I’ll collect all the posts together and sell it as a book during the 2016 Cosmic Nomad Tour… ### Recent Posts - News – Boston Buddies, Space Shuttles & Bottoming Out [Boston & NYC] - News – Diving between continents & hiking to desolation [Iceland] - News – Airport Hell, Involuntary Weight Loss, & UK Mars100 Meetup - News – Life in a Box, Festival Madness & Going Global - News – 2016 “Cosmic Nomad” Global Tour - News – The Martian Stunt #bringhimhome - SHSSP16 Week 3 – Fighting Flat Earthers, New Management & Cultured Chaos - SHSSP Week 2 – Goodbye Spaceman, Buzz Day & Payload Tension - SHSSP Week 1 – Droids, Starmen & Grabthar’s Hammer - News – That whole “Moving to the other side of the country” thing - News – Helena National Science Week Tour - Mars One – Parachuting & Media Mayhem - Mars Project – You Are Go To Continue Descent… - News – 2015: The Year Space Kicks It Up a Notch - Random – Fringe World for People Who Aren’t Old & Boring - Random – An Open Letter to Myself in 2020 - News – There and back again… (Part 2: Australia) - News – There and back again… Part 1: Europe - News – NatSciWeek Wrap Up & Roll on Europe - Mars Project – Becoming Martian & Other Science Week Madness

item.title: Website - Parachuting & Media Mayhem
item.description:
7 Step Parachute Landing Fall

One of the first things you’re taught when you learn to parachute is how to land without breaking a leg. If you’re learning to free fall like I did, you’re eventually taught to pull down on the control handles and “flare” your parachute at just the right height for a smooth and soft landing. But the first landing you’re taught – and the only one you can use if something goes wrong or you’re using a round parachute – is a “PLF”, or Parachute Landing Fall.

item.description:
The last two and a half years have been pretty odd.

In September 2012 I started researching how to send people one-way to Mars for a comedy show, and found an organisation aiming to do it for real.
In 2013 I was one of 202,586 people who applied to be on the first crew to go, and one of 1058 short-listed for it.
In 2014 I was one of 705 that passed the medical selection, and one of 660 offered an interview.

item.title: Website – There and back again… Part 1 Europe
item.description: AUTHOR’S NOTE: I’ve broken this up into two posts because the original was just waaaay too big. “Part 2: Australia” will be published once my fingers recover. Looking back, the last Mighty Ginge update was August 29th: to say a lot has happened since seeing Chris Hadfield in Canberra is a gross understatement. You probably could have followed some of it via the fairly consistent  Instagram, Facebook & Twitter updates, but here’s my vague attempt to sum up the two months of utter chaos that was the European & Australian tour of Becoming Martian. **Germany (August 29th-September 1st) ** Meet “Identity Crisis Bear” Berlin was supposed to be a breather. But coming off the flight from Doha what it really devolved into was a mad dash to try to find three things: 1. WiFi to write & submit a proposal for a payload on a Mars lander 2. A printer to print my train ticket onward to Cologne 3. Food/Sleep In that order of priority. The initial submission deadline for Mars One’s University Competition was August 31st, so I had 24 hours to write an outline for the Helena payload – a scientific payload proposal to generate oxygen from the water in the Martian soil, that also includes a digital art library to Mars. In the process of trying to find wifi to access the payload reference documents I got to wander around Berlin a little, but since I’d visited before in late 2006 I was primarily just trying to find a cafe that I didn’t need a translator to ask for the wifi password… Even with the help of some friendly German cafes, the proposal still wasn’t written by the time I needed to board the train to Cologne. So I ended up writing and submitting a payload proposal for a Mars lander minutes before the deadline using the wifi on the train as it raced through the German countryside at over 230km/hr… Welcome to the future In Cologne I was back in more familiar territory, having stayed there for a few days last November while visiting Europe for the 2013 Living On Mars Convention. Not that I had time to enjoy the familiar sights – I crashed as soon as I checked in, and was up early the next day to visit the European Astronaut Centre! Do you know the way to astronaut street? One of my fellow Mars One candidates Andrea Boyd is EUROCOM – the European Space Agency’s communicator to the International Space Station. So she invited me to see where the European Space Agency’s astronauts train for expeditions to the space station, and where I could muck around in a Soyuz simulator… Not pictured: Hypoxia-induced hallucinations of George Clooney Netherlands (September 2nd – 8th) There was actually a day or two during the week in the Netherlands where I didn’t have to rush anywhere… but it sure as hell wasn’t the day I arrived. There was barely enough time to drop off my bag in Rotterdam before it was back on a train to The Hague – just making it in time for an event on solar weather hosted by the Netherlands Space Society, featuring ESA Astronaut Andre Kuipers and  World Space Week ‘s Executive Director  Remco Timmermans. Aurora expeditions with Remco Friday brought more space madness, meeting up with ESA’s Communications Director Juan De Dalmau for a tour of the European Space Research and Technology Centre (ESTEC) with fellow International Space University alumni. Me being a “Price Is Right” showgirl for ESA’s next spaceship The ESTEC visit had to be cut short though, because the same night the all important Redhead Days festival kicked off. I’d been in the Netherlands a month too late in 2013, so this year was a great chance to catch up with some old faces and see just how much the festival has grown since I last attended in 2012. Redhead Days Launch To be fair I was pretty burnt out by the time I got there, but something with Redhead Days also seemed to have shifted. The atmosphere of having so many redheads in one place from all across the world is still absolutely amazing, but it wasn’t quite the life altering event my first visit was. I’m certainly not the same person I was when I arrived lost at Breda train station two years ago, so maybe it shouldn’t have come as a surprise that there wasn’t the same impact coming back. The pub crawl continued to be the best event of the weekend’s official program, and this year there was the added bonus of trying to meetup for an interview with a French TV crew during it – they eventually found me (slightly more sober) the next day. But the real highlight was ticking off #22 on the 101 Things To Do Before You Die list by going up in a hot-air balloon the Monday the festival finished. Our balloon was obviously the one with the giant smiley face It was brilliant being back for the Redhead Days festival, but more importantly this visit closed out a lot of unfinished business in the Netherlands from the last 2 years. Maybe one day I’ll go back again for a bit of a laugh, but it very much feels like the festival did what it needed to do – starting my transition from a successful but half-hearted comedian, into a fully fledged space advocate. Ireland (September 9th – 14th) If the Netherlands was about closing out unfinished business, Ireland was very much about starting afresh. I’ve been providing support (viaSkype ) to Niamh Shaw as she developed her Dublin Fringe show, so when I found out the premiere of “To Space” was the night after the Redhead Days festival finished I knew it was the perfect chance to finally visit Ireland! Niamh’s premiere was amazing, and it was great to meet so many fantastic people from Ireland’s burgeoning space industry at the drinks afterwards. When Space Gingers Attack One of the completely unexpected parts of the evening was Niamh drawing names out of a hat to win a piece of original space art from Clare Henderson, and suddenly finding I had to tick off another entry from the 101 Things To Do Before You Die list: #92 Own an Original Work of Art Now safely mounted on my office wall The 48 hours in Dublin was awesome, but with only another 4 days to see as much of Ireland as possible it was into the hire car and off to Cork! Fellow Redhead festival-goer Irene had come over to Ireland too, so we shot down to Cork and met up with Joleen Cronin – organiser of the Irish Redhead Festival. Welcome to the Red-olution We also discovered that Cork is infact a magical and never-ending series of multi-story carparks, after inadvertently driving into 4 of them… Endless, ENDLESS, carparks Depending on how everything pans out with Mars One in the next 6 months, there’s a good chance I’ll be heading back to Cork for the 2015 Irish Redhead Festival to lead their “Ginger Ukulele Orchestra”. Whether I’ll be too busy with training to colonise another planet – or if this planet is ready for hundreds of gingers to start playing ukulele together – remains to be seen… Next stop on the flying Irish tour was the Ring of Kerry, where we witnessed panoramas like this: So… pretty… As well as some blatant racism towards my proud gold-loving cousins: As if we need a special crossing point – we’ve got enough gold to OWN the road Driving on to Dingle Bay, the leprechaun abuse stopped but the overwhelming pretty didn’t: View from the hostel’s balcony The western coast of Ireland – please collect your jaw before you leave Most of the time in Kerry & Dingle Bay was spent just trying not to have an aneurysm over the scenery, and we barely saw 1/100th of what the Wild Atlantic Way had to offer. But there was one really important historical stop we managed to squeeze in. Tom Crean  was an Irish explorer that partook in some of the greatest Antarctic expeditions of all time: leading a team on Scott’s 1902 Discovery expedition, surviving Scott’s fatal follow-up  Terra Nova expedition in 1910, as well as Shackleton’s ill-fated Endurance expedition. But once Crean had earned his  3rd polar medal & served a further 4 years with the Royal Navy, he retired to Annascaul… where he opened a pub. This is a real place that serves “Crean’s Lager”. We had Coke Four days in Ireland isn’t even remotely enough to even explore Dublin properly, let alone Cork, Kerry & Dingle Bay. But Irene had to head back to the US for work and I was off to Northern Ireland for the CultureTECH Festival. We stayed back in Dublin with Niamh Shaw on our last night in Ireland though, and ended the Ireland leg of the trip with Niamh giving me what is easily the best LEGO set ever: XCOR’s Lynx Mark II CultureTECH in Derry, Northern Ireland (September 15th – 19th) The CultureTECH festival in Derry  was always going to be the trip’s pressure pot – 3 days as one of the featured speakers for a technology festival with hundreds of events & activities. I wound up staying for 5 days: speaking about Mars One at half a dozen schools that ranged from high-end boarding schools, to running technology workshops, playing Bowie’s “Space Oddity” on ukulele during interviews with BBC radio, performing “Becoming Martian” as a charity event for Children In Crossfire, and talking about having the courage to fail  over and over and over again at the Create2014 student-run event. Create2014 – Inspirin’ da yoof with failure It was 5 days of abject chaos… but without a doubt one of the best parts of the entire trip. Because while I was running around like a headless chook trying to keep track of when and where I was, every step of the way there were incredible people to steer me in the right direction. The team from CultureTECH were simply amazing: lining up as many school visits as I could squeeze in, organising interviews with the BBC, and having taxis ready to get me wherever I needed to be. Not only that, they put me up in 5-star accommodation the whole time I was there so I could tick off a third entry from the 101 Things list: #30 “Stay in the Best Suite in a Five Star Hotel”. It wasn’t just the CultureTECH organisers who were awesome either. My old Irish friend Barry had moved back to Derry a few months before, so it was fantastic to finally catch up with him – I’d barely seen Barry since late 2010, when we were sharing a mouldy flat in London and I moved out because my taste in girlfriends had suddenly improved. Without going into specifics Barry has had a particularly rough year, so I think it was good for both of us to catch up and remember that even with the dips he’s had over the last 12 months, life is still way better than it was 4 years ago. Circa December 2010, aka “Evidence Exhibit A” But while we were reminiscing, Barry & I were also causing chaos at the festival and making mountains of friends doing it. CultureTECH had brought in so many inspiring folks from all across the world it was hard to keep track of them all: Heather from Uproar Comics, Alastair from Startacus, the dozen scholarship winners from Honeycomb, and the hysterical team from Ministry of Science … whose children’s shows undoubtedly contain less innuendo than I like to pretend they do. Emma wants to end on a big bang, but Mike isn’t sure they should, in front of all the kids… CulutreTECH was genuinely out of control, and I loved every moment of it – from ridiculous dinner parties that ended with us getting kicked out of the dodgiest pub in Derry, right through to performing “Becoming Martian” while sounding like a koala with emphysema because my voice had gone that morning. It was ridiculous, fun-filled chaos all the way through, and I genuinely hope I get a chance to go back again and do it all again. London, Benenden & Brighton (Sept 20-26) Leaving Northern Ireland was a stark wake up call to the realities of life though… And let us never speak of this again After the nightmare that was my flight out of Belfast to Bristol though, I managed to knock over a bunch of little jobs that I’d been carrying with me since National Science Week. Restitching my bag, sewing patches on my ukulele case, copying all my random scraps of paper covered in ideas into something more permanent… general travel admin. Once you’ve been living out of a bag for a few weeks there’s often a moment where you realise things are going to start falling apart on you if you don’t take a little time to fix them – landing in Bristol was that moment, so on the bus to Bath I sorted everything. Things would start falling apart again before I got back to Perth, but that’s another story. The return to Gloucestershire was very short though. I managed to catch up with Vicky & Olly – two great friends from my days working for Damien Hirst – for a few hours in Bath. But the next morning the infamous Martin  picked me up for breakfast in my old town of Stroud, I managed to catch up with Mark Chatterley from InEarEntertainment for a few hours, then it was on the move again down to London that afternoon… For tourists, this is a delightful photo op. For anyone who’s spent 6 hours waiting for a 5am train, this sign causes a rash London was another rushed, overnight visit – caught up briefly with John &  Jo to see what wonderful things they’d been doing post Edinburgh Fringe, but the very next morning it was off to speak to the students at the exclusive Benenden boarding school in country Kent. The kids and staff were brilliant, really enthusiastic about World Space Week, and I even managed to find a fellow ukulele-er among the staff! The compulsion to play “Duelling Banjos” was significant But Benenden was really just a fun detour for where I really wanted to be, was here… Into the Temple of (burrito) Sacrifice … with it’s amazing interior decorations… Mexican eating establishment protected by The Space Jesus Last stop of the Europe leg was back to that other old stomping ground of mine: Brighton, with the best burritos on the planet at La Choza. The world’s best housemate, Megan – whose garage I was living in when I decided to sign up for Mars One at the end of September 2012 – put me up for a few nights while I prepared for the return to Australia, partaking in all the awesome food and coffee Brighton has to offer at the same time. And in amongst it all I even managed to get up to London again to catch up with Lizzy from Ginger Parrot  at an open mic cabaret night in an underground toilet. With all of that going on, you’d think it would be time to go home and have a bit of a nap. And if you call all of Australia home, then yeah I did go home – “home” to run a space conference in Adelaide, present at a different space conference, speak & perform at a Newcastle writer’s festival, dress up like an aluminium-foil covered robot with plastic cups for boobs, bolt up to Brisbane to speak at schools & universities, as well as meeting dozens more amazing people along the way. item.title: Website – 101 Things (2 Swim With…)
item.description:
If you’ve been diving with sharks since you were 12, you know filling in #2 of the 101 List (Swim With…) is always going to be a laugh.

Swim with… Sharks
Bronze Whaler - photographed near Gnaraloo Station April 2009 Diving regularly in Australia inevitably means being in the water with sharks of one type or another. But ultimately sharks get a really bad rap – at the end of the day they’re just another fish, and most of them terrified of humans. The only time I’ve ever felt threatened by sharks is when we’ve been spear-fishing (and having a fish bleed into the water) in areas where larger sharks are known to be common – it’s a calculated risk based on experience and healthy respect for animals that are only acting under instinct in their natural environment. But here’s a few of my more notable experiences with sharks. 8 foot Wobbegong Shark – Off the coast of Perth, October 1997 I’d completed my PADI Junior Open Water Course a few days after my 12th birthday, and my Dad (who’d been my instructor) had taken me out for several dives in the months since. On a few of these post-course dives we’d come across Port Jackson Sharks which were receptive to being held and patted. It might seem surreal to be 12 and holding a shark across your lap, patting it like a dog, but these “sharks” are quite harmless and are regularly found in aquarium touch pools.
And ADORABLE! Port Jackson’s do however have tails that could (if you’re 12) be confused with that of the much  larger and far more aggressive  Wobbegong – a carpet shark that (like Port Jackson’s) sit on the bottom of caves and  will leave a nasty bite. Also, they have teeth that hook backwards preventing them from letting go once they’ve bitten down. So not to be disturbed – for example – by a 12 year old scuba diver that’s seen just it’s tail sticking out of a cave, and tried to pull it out thinking it’s a Port Jackson. The wobby had swum into a cave then stuck his tail out through a hole in the reef. I’ve spotted the tail, thought it was a Port Jackson and tried to pull him out to say hello. And when he didn’t come out, I started pulling harder and harder… Dad turned around to see why I’d fallen behind, only to get the full view – seeing me standing on top of the reef pulling a shark’s tail, and being able to see the massive Wobbegong going mental underneath as I tried to drag a 4 foot wide animal out through a 1 foot hole. Dad started waving frantically to tell me to let go, so I did. The wobby took off like a rocket out from under the reef, straight toward Dad, only to swim right by him and off into the abyss. Needless to say, these days I like to check exactly what I’m dealing with before I go grabbing animal tails underwater. 15 foot Tiger Shark – Gnaraloo Fishing Station, April 2001 Gnaraloo has been an annual pilgrimage for my Dad and his diving/fishing mates since time began – every April they drive 12 hours to get there, sleep in a sheep shed for two weeks fishing and free-diving every day. By my first trip in 2001 I’d already had a bit of experience dealing with sharks while spear-fishing, and within a few days of being in Gnaraloo we’d been chased out of the water by an aggressive hammerhead that started circling and tried to eat the bag full of speared fish. But toward the end of the trip we had about an 8 foot Bronze Whaler (same species and similar size to the shark pictured at the top) swim into where we were spearing. You can usually tell when a shark is around because all the fish start to become scarce. There’s usually a few fish still swimming about though – but this time there eerily everything disappeared. And sure enough, Dad and I saw the Bronze Whaler and started to head back to the boat to move – there’s no point trying to spear fish if a shark is scaring them all away. And that’s when a 15 foot tiger shark loomed out of the darkness and bit the bronze whaler in half.
When the sharks start eating other sharks - YOU NEED TO GET OUT OF THE WATER I’d just like to point out that an 8 foot Bronze Whaler is a formidable shark in itself – while they’re not known to attack humans unprovoked, they do harass spear-fishers – as I’d discovered a month after the wobbegong, when Dad and I had finished a dive (in a place called “Shark Bay” strangely enough) with me latched onto Dad’s back as he was pushing away a circling 6 foot black tip shark with a speargun, while a 10 foot bronze-whaler shark swam around directly underneath us. So watching a tiger shark eat a Bronze-Whaler is enough to a) get you back in the boat in record time, and b) make you wonder if staying in the boat and fishing with a line for the rest of the trip might be a wise move. **Swim with…Whales 90 foot Blue Whale with calf – Ningaloo Reef, May 2008 I’d just started to get back into diving after a few years staying dry, and was about to complete my Divemaster’s qualification when I went on a trip to Exmouth to dive the Ningaloo Reef. We spent a day free-diving with whale sharks, the biggest fish in the world (and not whales). Having an enormous whale shark swim up from the depths straight toward you isn’t an experience you forget easily, and spending a full day swimming with them was amazing. We were incredibly lucky to do that alone. But it wasn’t until the end of the day, when all the boats were heading back to Exmouth, that the whale shark spotter aircraft that was radioing in the locations of the whale sharks spotted the day’s real treat – a blue whale and it’s calf. They were literally going the same way we were on our way back to Exmouth, so the 4 boat contingent maintained a safe distance and took turns individually moving in closer for a slightly better look. We kept our distance, but to say it was huge is an understatement – even the calf was longer than our boat. And while technically we didn’t swim with  the blue whale and it’s calf, I wouldn’t have wanted to. I was lucky enough to see a humpback and a calf a few years later, during a  tech dive on my Extended Range course, that decided to briefly swim by in the distance during a decompression stop. But nothing could compare to spending 15 minutes in a boat next to the largest species of animal ever known to have existed, purely by coincidence of timing. **Swim with…Dolphins Red Sea Dolphins – Eilat, August 17th 1995 In October 1994, Jordan and Israel signed a peace treaty and began opening their borders. My family was living in Aqaba – on the Jordanian side of the Red Sea – when it happened because Dad was working for King Hussein at the time. Being 9 and watching Israeli army engineers clearing land mines live on CNN, and knowing the engineers were the same black dots we could see in the distance from our balcony was a fairly surreal experience. But the opening of the border meant we could visit Eilat – the Israeli city directly opposite Aqaba. It was still pretty difficult to get permission to cross the border into Israel for the day (and Dad couldn’t come with us), so Mum only took my sister and I a couple of times. But the most memorable trip across the border was August 17th 1995, on my 10th birthday, when we visited Dolphin Reef  to swim with the dolphins. I’d paddled with dolphins at Monkey Mia when I was younger, but this was the first experience I’d ever had swimming with them. We spent most of the day there – I was in and out of the water with the dolphins, eating ice cream and drinking Coca Cola (Coke and Pepsi had drawn up battle lines too – you couldn’t buy Coke in Jordan, Pepsi couldn’t be found in Israel) and making the most of a completely surreal birthday.

item.title: Article - What's Your ppO2
item.description: There’s one thing watched by rebreather divers with greater concern above anything else - your partial pressure of oxygen, aka “ppO2”. No matter how extraordinary it feels breathing warm air with no bubbles, clearing deco far quicker than your open circuit buddies and drifting around gently to the sound of your own breath; it all comes at the cost of knowing the gas in your loop can quickly and easily become toxic if you’re not vigilantly watching your ppO2. If a solenoid sticks open or a manual add valve jams on, the flood of oxygen into the loop can drive your ppO2 over 1.60 and quickly lead to a hyperoxic convulsion that will ruin your whole day. On the flip side we need a ppO2 of about 0.18atm - equivalent to 18% oxygen on the surface - just to maintain regular brain function, and about 0.15 to maintain consciousness. And as I was brutally reminded earlier this year, ppO2 also happens to drop rather rapidly just as you approach the surface when you think the dive is over.
